title: Returning to Clay
summary: A return to wheel-thrown pottery connects current greenware studies to surviving wood-fired work from a Brookhaven apprenticeship three decades earlier.
searchSummary: Wheel-thrown pottery spanning circa 1994–1995 Brookhaven wood firing and a 2026 return to the same make and model of kickwheel, with current forms still unfired.
stage: Historical work archived; current apprenticeship in progress
recorded: Circa 1994–1995 work photographed in 2026; current practice documented from July 30, 2026.
sourceLabel: Returning to Clay journal and Pottery Flickr album

gallery.caption: The strongest surviving historical form: a tall jar thrown and wood-fired during the Brookhaven apprenticeship circa 1994–1995.
A pale wood-fired bowl from the same period shows the most resolved functional relationship among openness, rim, and fired surface.
An unfired Balcones Dark jar from the renewed practice, with an incised field carried across its lower volume.

introduction: Returning to clay after roughly thirty years is less a restart than a conversation with earlier work. The surviving wood-fired pots show both the material instincts worth recovering and the formal habits that the current apprenticeship is meant to sharpen.
evidenceBoundary: The current photographed vessels remain unfired greenware. The present Lockerbie Model K is the same make and model used in the 1990s, not the same physical wheel.
